name: OMK 2A Heme — Summative 3 Objective Review · Board-Style Set 4 (Hard)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the trauma bay after a motorcycle collision. He is hypotensive with a distended abdomen, and the massive transfusion protocol is activated. His blood type is not yet known. While uncrossmatched group O RhD-negative erythrocytes are being infused, the trauma surgeon requests plasma to be given simultaneously in a 1:1 ratio. The blood bank has group A, group B, group AB, and group O plasma immediately available. Which of the following should be selected, and why?
choices: A. Group AB plasma, because it contains neither anti-A nor anti-B antibody
B. Group AB plasma, because it lacks both A and B surface antigens
C. Group O plasma, because it contains both anti-A and anti-B antibody
D. Group O plasma, because it lacks both A and B surface antigens
E. Group-specific plasma must be withheld until the patient's ABO type is known
questions.explanation: Compatibility inverts between cellular and plasma products, and the reason is which half of the system the bag carries. RED CELLS carry ANTIGENS, so what matters is whether the recipient's antibodies will attack them: group O cells display neither A nor B antigen, so nobody's antibody has a target → group O is the universal RED CELL donor. PLASMA carries ANTIBODIES, so what matters is whether the donor's antibodies will attack the recipient's cells: group AB plasma contains neither anti-A nor anti-B, so it cannot attack any recipient's erythrocytes → group AB is the universal PLASMA donor. Note the symmetry that confirms you have understood rather than memorized it: group AB is the universal red cell RECIPIENT, and group O is the universal plasma RECIPIENT. Reconstructing the inversion from first principles is more reliable than recalling a table under pressure.

wrongExplanations.1: The statement about antigens is TRUE of group AB cells being unable to be given to others — but it is the wrong REASON for plasma. Plasma contains almost no cells and therefore almost no surface antigen; what makes AB plasma safe is the ABSENCE OF ANTIBODY, not the presence or absence of antigen.
wrongExplanations.2: Group O plasma is the most dangerous choice here for precisely the reason stated: it contains BOTH anti-A and anti-B. Infused into a group A, B, or AB recipient it would attack that patient's own erythrocytes. Group O is the universal plasma RECIPIENT, never the universal plasma donor.
wrongExplanations.3: This confuses the two products by applying the red cell rule to plasma. Group O lacking A and B antigens is exactly why group O CELLS are the universal donor — but antigen status is irrelevant to a plasma unit, whose hazard is its antibody content.
wrongExplanations.4: Withholding plasma during a massive transfusion protocol is the clinical error the protocol exists to prevent. When you bleed you lose WHOLE blood, so replacing only erythrocytes produces a dilutional coagulopathy; products are given in a balanced ratio from the outset, using universal-donor products until the type is known.

questions.eli5: Red cells carry markers on their surface, so you give the ones with no markers to anyone — type O. Plasma is the opposite: it carries the attacking antibodies, so you want the plasma that has none, which is type AB. The rule flips depending on which part of the blood is in the bag.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man taking dabigatran for atrial fibrillation is brought to the emergency department after falling down a flight of stairs. He is confused and has a large right parietal scalp hematoma. His pulse is 88/min and blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg. Glasgow Coma Scale score is 12. CT scan of the head shows a 2-cm acute subdural hematoma with early midline shift, and neurosurgery plans immediate evacuation. His last dose of dabigatran was 4 hours ago. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 218,000/mm3, a prothrombin time of 13 seconds (N=11–14), an activated partial thromboplastin time of 52 seconds (N=25–35), and a serum creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent to reverse his anticoagulation?
choices: A. Andexanet alfa
B. Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
C. Idarucizumab
D. Protamine sulfate
E. Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma
questions.explanation: Reversal is chosen by MECHANISM, so first identify the drug class. Dabigatran is a direct THROMBIN inhibitor — the only oral direct thrombin inhibitor in common use, and the outlier among the direct oral anticoagulants, which are otherwise factor Xa inhibitors. Its specific antidote is idarucizumab, a monoclonal antibody FRAGMENT that binds dabigatran with roughly 350 times the affinity thrombin does, neutralizing it within minutes. (A practical detail from the drug list: it is moisture-sensitive and must be kept in its original bottle.) Two features of the case support the need for reversal: his renal impairment prolongs dabigatran clearance, and the prolonged aPTT with a normal prothrombin time is consistent with thrombin inhibition. Reversal is indicated here because the bleeding is life-threatening and in a closed space, and surgery cannot wait.

wrongExplanations.0: Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent for the factor Xa INHIBITORS — apixaban and rivaroxaban. It is a modified, catalytically inactive factor Xa decoy that sequesters those drugs. It has no meaningful activity against a direct thrombin inhibitor, which binds a different enzyme entirely.
wrongExplanations.1: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate replaces factors II, VII, IX, and X and is the answer for urgent WARFARIN reversal. It is used off-label when a specific antidote is unavailable, but supplying more clotting factors does not remove a drug that directly inhibits thrombin, and a specific antidote exists here.
wrongExplanations.3: Protamine sulfate binds and neutralizes UNFRACTIONATED HEPARIN (with partial activity against low-molecular-weight heparin). He is not receiving heparin, and protamine has no affinity for dabigatran.
wrongExplanations.4: Vitamin K restores gamma-carboxylation of vitamin K-dependent factors and reverses WARFARIN over 6 to 24 hours; plasma is the fallback when prothrombin complex concentrate is unavailable. Both the mechanism and the timescale are wrong for a patient going to the operating room now, and dabigatran does not act on vitamin K metabolism.

questions.eli5: Different blood thinners need different antidotes, so the first job is naming which drug he is on. His works by blocking thrombin directly, and there is an antibody made specifically to grab that drug and pull it out of action within minutes. The antidote for the other common blood thinners would not touch it.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve is admitted for elective hip arthroplasty and is bridged with therapeutic subcutaneous enoxaparin while warfarin is held. She weighs 58 kg and her creatinine clearance is 62 mL/min. On hospital day 2 the covering resident notes that her activated partial thromboplastin time is 31 seconds (N=25–35) and is concerned that she is not adequately anticoagulated. She has had no bleeding and no thrombotic symptoms. Which of the following best explains this finding?
choices: A. Enoxaparin chains are too short to bridge antithrombin to thrombin, so the assay is insensitive to it
B. Enoxaparin has no effect on factor Xa and therefore does not alter any routine coagulation assay
C. Enoxaparin requires 5 to 7 days to reach steady state, so the anticoagulant effect is not yet measurable
D. Her creatinine clearance is high enough that the drug is cleared before it can exert an effect
E. Subcutaneous administration produces erratic absorption, making all laboratory monitoring unreliable
questions.explanation: Heparin has no intrinsic activity — it works by binding ANTITHROMBIN and accelerating it. But inhibiting THROMBIN and inhibiting FACTOR Xa require different things geometrically. To inactivate thrombin, the heparin chain must be long enough to form a bridge that holds antithrombin and thrombin together, which takes at least 18 saccharide units. To inactivate factor Xa, a conformational change in antithrombin alone suffices, and a short chain achieves that. Unfractionated heparin has long chains and does both, so it prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time and can be monitored with it. Low-molecular-weight heparins have SHORT chains: they still inhibit factor Xa but barely touch thrombin, so the activated partial thromboplastin time — a thrombin-dependent clotting assay — stays essentially normal even at full therapeutic dosing. A normal value therefore proves nothing. ANTI-Xa ACTIVITY is the only valid assay for enoxaparin and for fondaparinux (pure pentasaccharide, pure anti-Xa), and even then it is reserved for specific situations: renal impairment, extremes of body weight, and pregnancy.

wrongExplanations.1: This inverts the pharmacology. Factor Xa inhibition is exactly what enoxaparin DOES retain; what it largely loses relative to unfractionated heparin is anti-thrombin activity. It also does alter an assay — the anti-Xa assay.
wrongExplanations.2: Enoxaparin has a rapid, predictable onset with peak anti-Xa activity roughly 3 to 5 hours after a subcutaneous dose, and steady state within about a day. It is warfarin that takes days, because existing factors must decay first — which is precisely why she is being bridged.
wrongExplanations.3: A creatinine clearance of 62 mL/min is mildly reduced, and low-molecular-weight heparins are renally cleared, so impaired clearance would if anything cause ACCUMULATION and excess effect. Renal impairment is one of the recognized reasons to check an anti-Xa level.
wrongExplanations.4: Subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin has famously PREDICTABLE, dose-proportional pharmacokinetics with bioavailability above 90%. That reliability is the reason it can be given at a fixed weight-based dose without routine monitoring at all.

questions.eli5: Heparin works by holding a natural brake protein against its target. Blocking one target needs a long molecule to reach across and bridge them; blocking the other target does not. This short-chain version can only do the second job, so the usual clotting test barely changes even when the dose is correct.

questions.stem:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the office because of a swollen, painful left knee that developed overnight without injury. He has had two similar episodes involving the right ankle and the left elbow over the past year, and he bled for several hours after a tooth extraction at age 5. His mother's brother had a similar bleeding history. He takes no medications. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F). Physical examination shows a warm, distended left knee held in partial flexion with markedly limited range of motion. There are no petechiae and no mucosal bleeding. Laboratory studies show:

    Platelet count                              268,000/mm3
    Prothrombin time                            12 sec (N=11–14)
    Activated partial thromboplastin time       64 sec (N=25–35)
    Factor VIII activity                        92% (N=50–150)
    von Willebrand factor antigen               108% (N=50–150)

A 1:1 mixing study corrects the activated partial thromboplastin time, and the correction persists after 2 hours of incubation at 37°C. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: A. Factor IX deficiency
B. Factor XI deficiency
C. Factor XII deficiency
D. Hemophilia A
E. Von Willebrand disease, type 2
questions.explanation: Work the algorithm. WHERE he bleeds: hemarthrosis and deep muscle bleeding, with NO mucocutaneous bleeding, points to the coagulation cascade rather than to platelets or von Willebrand factor. WHICH ARM: a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal prothrombin time isolates the intrinsic pathway — factors VIII, IX, XI, and XII. MIXING STUDY: it corrects and STAYS corrected after incubation, so this is a true deficiency, not an inhibitor. Now eliminate: factor VIII activity is 92%, which excludes hemophilia A, and von Willebrand antigen is normal, which excludes von Willebrand disease. The X-LINKED pedigree — an affected maternal uncle, a healthy carrier mother, an affected son — fits the two X-linked hemophilias, and with factor VIII normal the answer is factor IX deficiency: hemophilia B, or Christmas disease. It is clinically indistinguishable from hemophilia A at the bedside and is separated only by factor assay; it is about six times rarer, at 1 in 30,000 males versus 1 in 5,000. Treatment is factor IX concentrate, not factor VIII.

wrongExplanations.1: Factor XI deficiency (hemophilia C) also prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time and corrects on mixing, but it is AUTOSOMAL — so it affects both sexes and would not produce this maternal-uncle pedigree. Its bleeding is typically milder, correlates poorly with the factor level, and often appears only after surgery or trauma rather than as spontaneous hemarthrosis. It is enriched in Ashkenazi Jewish populations.
wrongExplanations.2: Factor XII deficiency prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time — often markedly — and corrects on mixing, but it causes NO BLEEDING AT ALL. It is the classic incidental laboratory abnormality, and this child has severe recurrent joint bleeding.
wrongExplanations.3: Hemophilia A is the far more common X-linked hemophilia and fits the pedigree and the bleeding pattern perfectly. It is excluded by a single number: a factor VIII activity of 92% is normal, and hemophilia A requires it to be low.
wrongExplanations.4: Type 2 von Willebrand disease causes MUCOCUTANEOUS bleeding — epistaxis, menorrhagia, gum bleeding — not hemarthrosis, and it is autosomal. Here the von Willebrand antigen is normal at 108% and the factor VIII it carries is also normal, so both the quantitative and the functional pathway are intact.

questions.eli5: Bleeding into joints rather than from gums and noses points to the clotting-protein side rather than the platelet side. One clotting test was slow, and adding normal plasma fixed it, so he is simply missing a protein. The usual missing protein tested normal, so it is the next one along — a rarer form that looks identical but needs a different replacement.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with a history of recurrent sinopulmonary infections and intermittent diarrhea since childhood undergoes elective cholecystectomy. Two units of packed red blood cells are ordered for an intraoperative hemorrhage. Approximately 4 minutes after the transfusion is begun, and after roughly 5 mL has been infused, she develops flushing, generalized urticaria, stridor, and hypotension. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 138/min, and blood pressure is 62/38 mm Hg. There is no fever, no back or flank pain, and her plasma is clear rather than pink. A direct antiglobulin test performed after the reaction is negative. Which of the following is the most likely underlying predisposing condition?
choices: A. Bruton agammaglobulinemia
B. Chronic granulomatous disease
C. Common variable immunodeficiency with anti-IgA antibodies
D. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
E. Selective IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies
questions.explanation: Three features define this as ANAPHYLAXIS rather than any other transfusion reaction: it began within minutes, it followed a TINY volume (classically about 5 mL, and dose-independence is the hallmark), and it is urticaria plus airway compromise plus hypotension with NO FEVER. The stem then rules out the competitors explicitly — no fever excludes febrile nonhemolytic and septic reactions, and clear plasma with a negative antiglobulin test excludes acute hemolysis. The mechanism is IgA. Every plasma-containing product contains IgA. A patient who produces no IgA can form ANTI-IgA antibodies, and on re-exposure those trigger anaphylaxis. Selective IgA deficiency is the MOST COMMON primary immunodeficiency, is frequently asymptomatic or causes exactly this pattern of recurrent respiratory and gastrointestinal infection, and is associated with autoimmune disease and allergy. Management is immediate epinephrine and airway support, and lifelong provision of WASHED or IgA-deficient products.

wrongExplanations.0: Bruton agammaglobulinemia is an X-linked defect of Bruton tyrosine kinase and would be extraordinarily unlikely in a woman. It causes an absence of essentially ALL immunoglobulin classes with absent tonsils and atrophic lymph nodes, presenting in infancy — and a patient who makes no IgG cannot readily mount the anti-IgA antibody this reaction requires.
wrongExplanations.1: Chronic granulomatous disease is a PHAGOCYTE disorder — absent NADPH oxidase, with recurrent abscesses and infections by catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia, and Aspergillus. Immunoglobulin levels are normal and there is no association with transfusion anaphylaxis.
wrongExplanations.2: Common variable immunodeficiency is the most tempting alternative: it causes recurrent sinopulmonary infection and gastrointestinal disease in a young adult, and some patients do have anti-IgA antibodies. It is distinguished by LOW IgG with low IgA and/or IgM and impaired vaccine responses, whereas the classic and far more common transfusion-anaphylaxis association is with an ISOLATED IgA deficiency in a patient whose other immunoglobulins are normal.
wrongExplanations.3: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria causes complement-mediated INTRAVASCULAR HEMOLYSIS from absent CD55 and CD59, with hemoglobinuria and a very high lactate dehydrogenase. It would produce pink plasma and dark urine, both of which are explicitly absent, and it does not cause anaphylaxis.

questions.eli5: She reacted violently to just a teaspoon of blood, with hives and a closing airway but no fever — that pattern is an allergic reaction, not a mismatch. She was born without one class of antibody, so her body treats that antibody as foreign when it arrives in donated plasma. She needs blood that has been washed free of it.

questions.stem: A newborn girl delivered at 34 weeks' gestation to a 29-year-old woman is severely edematous at birth with marked ascites, pleural effusions, and pallor, and requires immediate intubation. The placenta is bulky. The mother received no prenatal care. Her blood type is A, RhD-positive, and an antibody screen is negative. The infant's blood type is A, RhD-positive, and a direct antiglobulin test is negative. Cord blood studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 5.8 g/dL and hemoglobin electrophoresis shows predominantly a tetramer of gamma globin chains with no hemoglobin A and no hemoglobin F. Both parents are of Southeast Asian ancestry and each has a mild microcytic anemia that has never responded to iron. Which of the following best explains this infant's condition?
choices: A. Deletion of all four alpha globin genes
B. Deletion of three alpha globin genes
C. Homozygous beta globin point mutations
D. Maternal anti-D alloimmunization
E. Maternal parvovirus B19 infection
questions.explanation: Start from the gene arithmetic, which drives the whole thalassemia framework. Adult hemoglobin is alpha-2 beta-2. You have FOUR alpha genes (two on each copy of chromosome 16) but only TWO beta genes (one on each copy of chromosome 11) — an asymmetry that explains why alpha thalassemia comes in four graded severities while beta thalassemia does not. Delete all four alpha genes and NO functional hemoglobin can be made at any stage of life, because alpha chains are required for fetal hemoglobin (alpha-2 gamma-2) as well as adult. The unpaired gamma chains instead self-associate into a gamma-4 tetramer — hemoglobin Barts — which has extremely high oxygen affinity and essentially never releases oxygen to tissues. The result is profound intrauterine hypoxia, high-output failure, and hydrops fetalis, exactly as described. Two supporting clues: Southeast Asian ancestry, where the cis-deletion that makes this possible is prevalent, and two parents with lifelong iron-unresponsive microcytosis, each carrying a two-gene deletion. The negative antiglobulin test and matched RhD status exclude immune hydrops and force a non-immune explanation.

wrongExplanations.1: A three-gene deletion is hemoglobin H disease. One alpha gene remains, so some functional hemoglobin is made and the child survives — with a chronic hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly, and beta-4 tetramers (hemoglobin H) rather than gamma-4. It does not cause hydrops fetalis.
wrongExplanations.2: Beta globin mutations cannot present at birth with hydrops, because the fetus is making fetal hemoglobin (alpha-2 gamma-2), which contains NO beta chains. Beta thalassemia major therefore declares itself at around 6 months, as the gamma-to-beta switch completes — the same reason sickle cell disease is not symptomatic in the newborn.
wrongExplanations.3: Anti-D alloimmunization causes IMMUNE hydrops and is excluded three ways here: the mother is RhD-POSITIVE and so cannot make anti-D, her antibody screen is negative, and the infant's direct antiglobulin test is negative.
wrongExplanations.4: Parvovirus B19 does cause non-immune hydrops by infecting erythroid progenitors and producing severe fetal anemia. But it would not alter hemoglobin electrophoresis at all — the infant would make normal fetal hemoglobin, simply not enough of it — and it would not explain two parents with inherited microcytosis.

questions.eli5: Everyone has four copies of one hemoglobin gene and only two of the other, which is why the first kind comes in degrees of severity. This baby inherited no working copies at all, so she could not build usable hemoglobin even before birth. The leftover chains stuck together into a form that grabs oxygen and refuses to hand it over.

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old man comes to the office because of a 6-month history of increasing fatigue, early satiety, and drenching night sweats. He has lost 8 kg (18 lb). He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows conjunctival pallor and a firm spleen palpated 12 cm below the left costal margin. There is no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  8.2 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  25%
    Leukocyte count             14,200/mm3
    Platelet count              96,000/mm3
    Lactate dehydrogenase       620 U/L

A peripheral blood smear shows teardrop-shaped erythrocytes, nucleated erythrocytes, and occasional myelocytes and metamyelocytes. Repeated attempts at bone marrow aspiration yield no material. A core biopsy specimen shows extensive reticulin fibrosis with clusters of atypical, hyperchromatic megakaryocytes. Testing for BCR-ABL1 is negative and JAK2 V617F is positive. Which of the following best explains this patient's peripheral smear findings?
choices: A. Autoimmune destruction of circulating erythrocytes
B. Distortion of marrow architecture forcing premature cell release
C. Hypersplenism sequestering mature cells
D. Ineffective erythropoiesis from a maturation defect
E. Mechanical fragmentation of erythrocytes in small vessels
questions.explanation: The combination of immature WHITE cells plus nucleated RED cells plus teardrop erythrocytes in the same smear is a LEUKOERYTHROBLASTIC picture, and it has a single meaning: the marrow architecture is disturbed. Cells are squeezed out through a scarred, distorted marrow-blood barrier before they are ready, and erythrocytes are physically deformed into teardrops (dacrocytes) as they are forced past fibrotic struts. The two things that do this are marrow SCARRING and marrow REPLACEMENT — here it is fibrosis, confirmed by the dry tap (fibrosis prevents aspiration, so a core biopsy is mandatory) and by reticulin deposition with atypical megakaryocytes. That is primary myelofibrosis: a JAK2-driven myeloproliferative neoplasm in which clonal megakaryocytes release platelet-derived growth factor and transforming growth factor beta, stimulating fibroblasts that are themselves NOT part of the malignant clone. Massive splenomegaly follows from extramedullary hematopoiesis — the fetal sites reopening under demand. BCR-ABL1 negativity separates it from chronic myeloid leukemia, and unlike its JAK2 relatives polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia, this one presents with marrow FAILURE rather than with excess.

wrongExplanations.0: Autoimmune hemolysis would give spherocytes with a positive direct antiglobulin test and a HIGH reticulocyte count. It produces no immature white cells, no nucleated erythrocytes, and no teardrop forms, and it would not cause a dry tap.
wrongExplanations.2: Hypersplenism genuinely contributes to his cytopenias — a spleen this large traps cells. But sequestration removes MATURE cells from the circulation; it cannot explain the appearance of IMMATURE white cells and nucleated red cells in the blood, nor the teardrop deformity, nor the fibrosis on biopsy.
wrongExplanations.3: Ineffective erythropoiesis — cells dying within the marrow — is the mechanism in megaloblastic anemia and myelodysplastic syndrome. It produces macrocytes or dysplastic forms with a hypercellular marrow that aspirates readily, not teardrops from a fibrotic marrow that will not aspirate at all.
wrongExplanations.4: Mechanical fragmentation in small vessels produces SCHISTOCYTES — angular helmet-shaped fragments — as in the thrombotic microangiopathies or around a prosthetic valve. Teardrops are elongated with a single point, a different deformity with a different cause, and there is no thrombocytopenic consumptive picture here.

questions.eli5: His bone marrow is filling up with scar tissue, so blood cells get squeezed out through a damaged, narrowed space before they are finished. Red cells get pulled into teardrop shapes on the way out, and immature cells escape early. His spleen has grown enormous because it restarted making blood to compensate.

questions.stem:
A 22-year-old man of Mediterranean ancestry comes to the emergency department because of fatigue, yellow eyes, and dark urine for 2 days. Five days ago he began trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. He has never had jaundice before. His temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 104/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and pallor; there is no splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  8.4 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  25%
    Mean corpuscular volume     89 μm3
    Reticulocyte count          5.8%
    Lactate dehydrogenase       610 U/L
    Total bilirubin             3.6 mg/dL
    Direct bilirubin            0.4 mg/dL
    Haptoglobin                 Undetectable (N=30–200 mg/dL)

A direct antiglobulin test is negative. A peripheral blood smear shows erythrocytes with a semicircular portion of the membrane missing, and supravital staining with crystal violet shows dark round intracellular inclusions. A quantitative enzyme assay performed on the day of presentation is reported as within the normal range. Which of the following best explains this normal enzyme result?
choices: A. Reticulocytes released during hemolysis have higher enzyme activity than older erythrocytes
B. The assay cannot be interpreted in the presence of an elevated bilirubin concentration
C. The enzyme is normal because the defect is in pyruvate kinase rather than in this pathway
D. The patient is a heterozygous female carrier with random X-inactivation
E. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole transiently induces enzyme synthesis
questions.explanation: Everything points to glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency: Mediterranean ancestry, an oxidant drug, acute intravascular hemolysis 2 to 5 days later, and the two morphologic signatures — BITE CELLS, where splenic macrophages have plucked out precipitated hemoglobin leaving a semicircular defect, and HEINZ BODIES, the precipitated denatured hemoglobin itself, visible only on supravital stain. The trap is the timing of the assay. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity DECLINES as an erythrocyte ages, so the enzyme-poorest cells are the oldest, and those are exactly the cells the oxidant destroys first. What survives — plus the flood of new reticulocytes the marrow is releasing, which are the youngest and most enzyme-rich cells of all — gives a falsely normal or even high result during an acute episode. The assay must therefore be REPEATED 2 to 3 MONTHS LATER, once the population has re-equilibrated. This is also why the disease is self-limited: hemolysis stops on its own as the vulnerable older cohort is cleared, even if the drug continues.

wrongExplanations.1: Hyperbilirubinemia can interfere with some spectrophotometric assays, but it is not the reason for a falsely normal result here, and a bilirubin of 3.6 mg/dL is modest. The explanation lies in which erythrocytes remain to be measured, not in optical interference.
wrongExplanations.2: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is a genuine hereditary enzymopathy, but it causes a chronic NONSPHEROCYTIC hemolytic anemia present from childhood, without oxidant triggers, and it produces no bite cells or Heinz bodies. It would also not explain a normal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase result being reported as the finding to interpret.
wrongExplanations.3: This patient is male, and the deficiency is X-LINKED — which is why it manifests fully in males with a single affected allele. Random X-inactivation does produce variable expression in heterozygous females and can complicate their testing, but it does not apply here.
wrongExplanations.4: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the oxidant TRIGGER of the hemolysis, not an inducer of the enzyme. Nothing about it raises glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity; the drug generates oxidative stress that the deficient cell cannot neutralize.

questions.eli5: The enzyme runs low in old red cells and high in brand-new ones. The oxidant drug destroyed all his old cells first, and his marrow poured out fresh ones — so when the lab measured the enzyme, it was mostly measuring the new cells that still have plenty. The test has to be repeated a few months later to get a true answer.

questions.stem:
A 19-year-old man comes to the office because of fatigue, easy bruising, and bleeding gums for 6 weeks. He has had two episodes of fever and a sore throat during that period. He worked in a furniture refinishing shop for 18 months and used solvents without respiratory protection. He takes no medications. His temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 106/min, and blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor, scattered petechiae over both legs, and gingival oozing. There is NO lymphadenopathy, NO hepatomegaly, and NO splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  7.2 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  22%
    Mean corpuscular volume     94 μm3
    Leukocyte count             1,400/mm3
      Segmented neutrophils     16%
    Platelet count              12,000/mm3
    Reticulocyte count          0.2%

A peripheral blood smear shows pancytopenia with normal-appearing cells and NO blasts, no teardrop forms, and no dysplastic changes. Bone marrow biopsy shows a markedly HYPOCELLULAR marrow consisting largely of fat with sparse residual hematopoietic elements and no fibrosis, no infiltrate, and no increase in blasts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: A. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
B. Aplastic anemia
C. Hairy cell leukemia
D. Myelodysplastic syndrome
E. Primary myelofibrosis
questions.explanation: Cellularity is the ratio of hematopoietic cells to fat, and it is the single most discriminating finding when a marrow is examined for pancytopenia. A HYPOCELLULAR marrow — mostly fat, few hematopoietic cells — with no blasts, no dysplasia, no fibrosis, and no infiltrate means the stem cell compartment has been destroyed or suppressed rather than replaced. That is aplastic anemia. The mechanism in most acquired cases is immune: cytotoxic T lymphocytes targeting hematopoietic stem cells, which is why immunosuppression with antithymocyte globulin and cyclosporine works, with allogeneic transplant curative in the young. Known triggers include benzene and organic SOLVENTS (his occupational exposure), chloramphenicol, other drugs, viral hepatitis, and radiation. Note the physical examination, which is doing real work here: the ABSENCE of lymphadenopathy and organomegaly argues against a proliferative or infiltrative process, because a marrow that has stopped producing does not enlarge anything.

wrongExplanations.0: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia certainly causes pancytopenia in this age group, but it replaces the marrow with blasts, giving a HYPERCELLULAR marrow with 20% or more blasts and usually blasts in the blood. It typically causes lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly, all three of which are explicitly absent.
wrongExplanations.2: Hairy cell leukemia is the most tempting alternative because it also causes pancytopenia and a DRY TAP. It is distinguished by prominent SPLENOMEGALY, cells with fine cytoplasmic projections, expression of CD11c, CD25, and CD103, and marrow INFILTRATION by those cells rather than an empty fatty marrow.
wrongExplanations.3: Myelodysplastic syndrome shares the pancytopenia and the low reticulocyte count, and is the closest laboratory mimic. It is excluded by the marrow: it is characteristically HYPERCELLULAR with DYSPLASTIC changes across lineages — production is wasted, not absent — whereas this marrow is empty and the cells present look normal.
wrongExplanations.4: Primary myelofibrosis also gives a dry tap, but for the opposite reason: the marrow is packed with reticulin FIBROSIS and atypical megakaryocytes. It produces massive splenomegaly and a leukoerythroblastic smear with teardrop cells, and the biopsy here explicitly shows no fibrosis.

questions.eli5: All three types of blood cell are low, so the problem is at the source rather than with any one cell line. Looking inside the bone showed mostly fat where blood-forming tissue should be — the factory is empty rather than taken over by something else. Solvent exposure is one of the known causes.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old woman comes to the office for evaluation of an abnormal complete blood count found before elective knee arthroplasty. She feels well. She has no history of bleeding, thrombosis, headache, visual change, or pruritus. She takes no medications and does not smoke. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities; there is no splenomegaly and no evidence of infection or inflammation. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                          14.1 g/dL
    Hematocrit                          42%
    Leukocyte count                     8,400/mm3
    Platelet count                      912,000/mm3
    Serum ferritin                      142 ng/mL
    C-reactive protein                  0.3 mg/dL (N<0.5)
    Erythrocyte sedimentation rate      8 mm/h

A repeat platelet count 6 weeks later is 948,000/mm3, and review of records shows counts above 700,000/mm3 on three occasions over the past 2 years. A peripheral blood smear shows numerous platelets including large forms. Testing for BCR-ABL1 is negative and JAK2 V617F is positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
choices: A. Correction of iron deficiency as the presumed reactive cause
B. Cytoreduction with hydroxyurea plus low-dose aspirin
C. Observation without cytoreduction or antiplatelet therapy
D. Plateletpheresis to lower the platelet count acutely
E. Therapeutic anticoagulation with apixaban
questions.explanation: First separate REACTIVE from CLONAL thrombocytosis, because reactive is far more common and needs no platelet-directed treatment. Reactive thrombocytosis is TEMPORARY and follows a driver — iron deficiency, infection, inflammation, malignancy, tissue damage, or asplenia. Here every driver is excluded: ferritin is normal, C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate are normal, there is no infection or inflammation, and critically the elevation is PERSISTENT over 2 years. Add JAK2 V617F positivity with BCR-ABL1 negativity and this is essential thrombocythemia — a myeloproliferative neoplasm producing normally differentiated cells in excess. The danger in this family of diseases is THROMBOSIS, not marrow failure: as the lecture puts it, a count above a million is 'a lot of fuel there to generate a clot.' Risk stratification drives therapy, and she is HIGH RISK on two counts — age over 60 and a platelet count above 1 million approaching — so she receives cytoreduction with hydroxyurea plus low-dose aspirin. Low-risk patients (under 60, no prior thrombosis, no JAK2) may be managed with aspirin alone or observation.

wrongExplanations.0: Iron deficiency is one of the commonest causes of a REACTIVE thrombocytosis and is always worth excluding — which the stem does, with a normal ferritin of 142 ng/mL. Correcting an absent deficiency would accomplish nothing.
wrongExplanations.2: Observation would be reasonable for a genuinely low-risk patient — under 60, no prior thrombosis, no JAK2 mutation, and a lower count. She is 58 but has a persistently near-million count with a JAK2 mutation and is about to undergo arthroplasty, a strongly prothrombotic event, so leaving her untreated accepts an avoidable thrombotic risk.
wrongExplanations.3: Plateletpheresis lowers the count within hours and is reserved for ACUTE emergencies — an evolving stroke, a myocardial infarction, or life-threatening bleeding from acquired von Willebrand disease at extreme counts. It is a temporizing measure in an asymptomatic outpatient and does not treat the clone.
wrongExplanations.4: Therapeutic anticoagulation treats an established clot. The thrombotic risk here is platelet-driven and arterial as much as venous — a white, platelet-rich clot calls for an ANTIPLATELET agent plus cytoreduction, not a factor Xa inhibitor in a patient who has never had a thrombosis.

questions.eli5: A high platelet count usually just means the body is reacting to something else, like low iron or an infection — but all of those were checked and normal, and hers has stayed high for two years. A gene test confirmed her bone marrow is making them on its own. That many platelets is fuel for a clot, so the count gets lowered and a low-dose aspirin added.

questions.stem:
A 3-day-old boy born at home at term is brought to the emergency department because of bleeding from the umbilical stump and blood in his stool. The mother declined all newborn prophylaxis and screening. He has been exclusively breastfed. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 158/min, and respirations are 44/min. Physical examination shows oozing from the umbilical stump, a large scalp hematoma, and scattered ecchymoses over the trunk. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                                  11.8 g/dL
    Platelet count                              288,000/mm3
    Prothrombin time                            38 sec (N=11–14)
    Activated partial thromboplastin time       76 sec (N=25–35)
    Fibrinogen                                  262 mg/dL (N=200–400)
    D-dimer                                     Within normal limits

Which of the following best explains these findings?
choices: A. Consumption of coagulation factors from disseminated intravascular coagulation
B. Deficiency of factor VIII from hemophilia A
C. Impaired gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X
D. Maternal autoantibody crossing the placenta and destroying platelets
E. Quantitative deficiency of von Willebrand factor
questions.explanation: Both the prothrombin time and the activated partial thromboplastin time are markedly prolonged, while the platelet count and FIBRINOGEN are entirely normal and the D-dimer is normal — that combination points to a deficiency of multiple factors WITHOUT consumption. Vitamin K is the cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which adds a carboxyl group to glutamate residues on factors II, VII, IX, and X (and on proteins C and S), allowing them to bind calcium and anchor to phospholipid membranes. Newborns are uniquely vulnerable on three counts: vitamin K crosses the placenta poorly, the gut is not yet colonized by the bacteria that synthesize it, and BREAST MILK contains very little (formula is supplemented). Without the intramuscular vitamin K given at birth — declined here — classic hemorrhagic disease of the newborn appears at 2 to 7 days, with umbilical, gastrointestinal, cutaneous, and in the worst case intracranial bleeding. Treatment is parenteral vitamin K, plus fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate for active serious bleeding, since vitamin K alone takes hours to work.

wrongExplanations.0: Disseminated intravascular coagulation would also prolong both clotting times, but it CONSUMES fibrinogen and platelets and generates fibrin degradation products. His fibrinogen is 262 mg/dL, his platelet count is 288,000/mm3, and his D-dimer is normal — all three findings exclude consumption and are the reason they are given.
wrongExplanations.1: Hemophilia A prolongs only the activated partial thromboplastin time and leaves the prothrombin time NORMAL, because factor VIII sits in the intrinsic pathway alone. His prothrombin time of 38 seconds cannot be explained by it. Hemophilia also does not typically cause umbilical stump bleeding.
wrongExplanations.3: Neonatal alloimmune or autoimmune thrombocytopenia causes petechiae and bleeding from maternal antibody against fetal platelets, but it produces a LOW PLATELET COUNT with normal clotting times. His platelet count is normal and his clotting times are grossly abnormal — the opposite pattern.
wrongExplanations.4: Von Willebrand disease causes MUCOCUTANEOUS bleeding with a normal or only mildly prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time and a normal prothrombin time. Even severe type 3 disease, which lowers factor VIII secondarily, would not prolong the prothrombin time.

questions.eli5: Babies are born with very little vitamin K, their gut bacteria have not arrived to make it, and breast milk contains almost none — which is why every newborn normally gets a shot at birth. Without it, several clotting proteins cannot be finished off and stay non-functional. Both clotting tests are slow while platelets and clotting fuel are normal, which points straight at the vitamin.

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old woman with a prosthetic aortic valve is admitted with Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis and begins high-dose intravenous penicillin G. On hospital day 9 she develops fatigue and jaundice. She has had no fever spikes for 4 days and repeat blood cultures are sterile. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 98/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus; the spleen is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  7.6 g/dL (11.9 g/dL on admission)
    Hematocrit                  23%
    Reticulocyte count          8.2%
    Lactate dehydrogenase       540 U/L
    Total bilirubin             3.4 mg/dL
    Direct bilirubin            0.4 mg/dL
    Haptoglobin                 Undetectable (N=30–200 mg/dL)

A direct antiglobulin test is POSITIVE for IgG. A peripheral blood smear shows spherocytes and no schistocytes. An eluate prepared from her erythrocytes reacts with donor cells ONLY in the presence of penicillin. Which of the following best explains this patient's anemia?
choices: A. Antibody directed against a drug bound to the erythrocyte membrane
B. Complement-mediated lysis by a cold-reacting IgM autoantibody
C. Mechanical fragmentation of erythrocytes by the prosthetic valve
D. Suppression of erythropoiesis by ongoing systemic infection
E. Warm autoantibody directed against an intrinsic erythrocyte antigen
questions.explanation: The eluate is the whole question. An eluate strips antibody off the patient's erythrocytes and asks what it recognizes. Here it reacts with donor cells ONLY when penicillin is present — so the antibody's target is not an erythrocyte antigen at all, but the DRUG. High-dose penicillin binds covalently to the erythrocyte membrane as a HAPTEN; IgG antibodies form against the drug-membrane complex, coat the cell, and splenic macrophages strip membrane from the opsonized cells, producing spherocytes and extravascular hemolysis. This is drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia of the hapten type, and the treatment is simply to STOP THE DRUG — the hemolysis then resolves, since removing the antigen removes the target. Distinguishing it from a true warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia matters, because the latter would call for corticosteroids and a much longer course. Other drugs work by different immune mechanisms — cephalosporins, quinine, and quinidine among them — and methyldopa classically induces a genuine autoantibody against Rh antigens.

wrongExplanations.1: A cold-reacting IgM autoantibody would give a direct antiglobulin test positive for COMPLEMENT C3d and negative for IgG, with acrocyanosis on cold exposure and erythrocyte clumping on a room-temperature smear. Her test is positive for IgG, and there is no cold-related history.
wrongExplanations.2: A prosthetic valve can shear erythrocytes and cause macroangiopathic hemolysis, and she has one — making this a genuinely tempting option. It is excluded by the smear and the serology: mechanical hemolysis produces SCHISTOCYTES (explicitly absent) and a NEGATIVE direct antiglobulin test, because no antibody is involved.
wrongExplanations.3: Anemia of inflammation from her endocarditis would develop gradually with a LOW reticulocyte count, normal bilirubin, and a normal haptoglobin. Her reticulocyte count of 8.2%, undetectable haptoglobin, and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia all indicate active destruction, not suppressed production.
wrongExplanations.4: A warm autoantibody is the closest competitor: it also gives spherocytes, extravascular hemolysis, and an IgG-positive direct antiglobulin test. It is separated by exactly one result — its eluate would react with donor cells WITHOUT any drug present, because the target is an intrinsic erythrocyte antigen. Hers reacts only when penicillin is added.

questions.eli5: The antibiotic stuck itself onto the surface of her red blood cells, and her immune system built antibodies against the drug — destroying the cells it was attached to. The lab proved it by showing her antibody only recognizes red cells when the drug is present. Stopping the antibiotic stops the destruction.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man comes to the office because of painless enlargement of lymph nodes in the neck, axillae, and groin, noticed over the past 8 months and slowly increasing. He feels well and has had no fever, night sweats, or weight loss. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows nontender cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy with nodes up to 3 cm, and a spleen palpated 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 13.6 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 7,200/mm3 with a normal differential, a platelet count of 232,000/mm3, and a lactate dehydrogenase of 198 U/L. Excisional biopsy of a cervical node shows effacement of architecture by closely packed nodular aggregates of small cleaved cells. Immunohistochemistry is positive for CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL2, and negative for CD5 and cyclin D1. The proliferation index is 8%. Cytogenetic studies show t(14;18). Which of the following best describes the expected clinical course?
choices: A. A rapidly progressive course that is highly curable with combination chemotherapy
B. A rapidly progressive course with a high risk of early tumor lysis and a low cure rate
C. An indolent course that is usually cured by a single course of chemotherapy
D. An indolent course with repeated response and relapse, and a low likelihood of cure
E. Spontaneous resolution without treatment in the majority of patients
questions.explanation: Two findings set the tempo. t(14;18) juxtaposes BCL2 to the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer, and BCL2 is an ANTI-APOPTOTIC gene — so these cells accumulate because they FAIL TO DIE, not because they divide quickly. The proliferation index of 8% confirms it. That gives follicular lymphoma, and it explains the paradox that governs lymphoma therapy: chemotherapy kills DIVIDING cells, so a tumor whose cells mostly sit still is never fully exposed to the drug. Follicular lymphoma therefore responds, relapses, and responds again over many years, and is generally NOT cured — while aggressive lymphomas with a high proliferation fraction, despite killing untreated patients in months, are destroyed almost entirely and ARE cured. Less differentiated means more aggressive means more curable; more differentiated means indolent means incurable. His immunophenotype confirms the diagnosis: CD10 and BCL2 positive with CD5 and cyclin D1 negative separates it from chronic lymphocytic leukemia and mantle cell lymphoma, the two CD5-positive neoplasms. Asymptomatic low-burden disease is often simply watched.

wrongExplanations.0: A rapidly progressive but curable course describes diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, which would show sheets of LARGE cells with a high proliferation index and typically a raised lactate dehydrogenase and B symptoms. His cells are small and cleaved, his index is 8%, and his lactate dehydrogenase is normal.
wrongExplanations.1: This describes a highly aggressive lymphoma such as Burkitt, which carries t(8;14) driving MYC and a near-100% proliferation index — and, being highly curable, does not fit 'a low cure rate' either. The tumor lysis risk is real in such disease precisely because of that rapid turnover, but it does not apply to a tumor with an 8% index.
wrongExplanations.2: No indolent lymphoma is cured by a single course of chemotherapy — that is precisely the point of the tempo rule. Cure requires exposing nearly the whole malignant population to a cytotoxic mechanism, which slow division prevents.
wrongExplanations.4: Spontaneous regression can occasionally occur in follicular lymphoma and in a few other settings, but it is uncommon and unpredictable, and it is not the expected course. The characteristic history is exactly what he describes — slow, painless, progressive adenopathy over months to years.

questions.eli5: These cancer cells are not multiplying fast — they are piling up because a broken switch stops them from dying on schedule. Chemotherapy kills cells while they divide, so a tumor that mostly sits still is hard to wipe out. It shrinks with treatment and comes back, again and again, over many years.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department from a nursing facility because of confusion and decreased urine output for 12 hours. She has a chronic indwelling urinary catheter. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102.0°F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 84/48 mm Hg. She is lethargic and oriented to person only. Physical examination shows warm extremities with bounding pulses and suprapubic tenderness. Urinalysis shows numerous leukocytes and bacteria. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 21,600/mm3, a serum creatinine of 2.6 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), and a serum lactate of 4.8 mmol/L (N=0.5–2.2). Blood pressure remains 86/50 mm Hg after 30 mL/kg of crystalloid. Which of the following best explains why the serum lactate is measured and repeated in this patient?
choices: A. It confirms the presence of bacteremia, which blood cultures may fail to demonstrate in 30% to 50% of cases
B. It distinguishes a gram-negative from a gram-positive organism as the causative pathogen
C. It identifies the cellular and metabolic derangement that, with circulatory failure, defines septic shock
D. It predicts which patients will require vasopressor therapy rather than fluid resuscitation alone
E. It quantifies the degree of renal impairment more sensitively than the serum creatinine does
questions.explanation: The definitions are nested, and each step adds exactly one requirement. Infection and bacteremia are RISK FACTORS — the setup, not the diagnosis. Add life-threatening ORGAN DYSFUNCTION from a dysregulated host response and it is SEPSIS. Add circulatory AND cellular/metabolic abnormalities profound enough to substantially increase mortality and it is SEPTIC SHOCK. That last definition is the key: septic shock is NOT simply hypotension. It requires both a circulatory component (persistent hypotension needing vasopressors despite adequate fluid resuscitation, as here) AND a cellular/metabolic component — which is what the lactate measures. Elevated lactate reflects tissue hypoperfusion and impaired cellular oxygen utilization, and that is precisely why lactate sits in the treatment bundle and why it is REPEATED: clearance over the first hours tracks whether resuscitation is working. The framing that organizes all of this is that sepsis is the HOST RESPONSE rather than the organism — which is also why no single organism defines it and why no criterion has adequate sensitivity or specificity on its own.

wrongExplanations.0: The statistic is correct — cultures are negative in 30% to 50% of sepsis cases, because the damage comes from the host response rather than from the pathogen directly. But lactate does not confirm bacteremia; it is a marker of tissue perfusion and is elevated in many non-infectious shock states.
wrongExplanations.1: Lactate rises with tissue hypoperfusion regardless of the organism, and gives no information about gram stain characteristics or species. Identification requires culture and susceptibility testing.
wrongExplanations.3: Lactate does carry prognostic weight, and higher values predict worse outcomes — but its role in the definition is diagnostic rather than predictive. This patient already meets the vasopressor criterion by remaining hypotensive after 30 mL/kg of fluid, so the lactate is not being used to forecast that.
wrongExplanations.4: Lactate and creatinine measure different things. Creatinine reflects glomerular filtration; lactate reflects global tissue perfusion and cellular metabolism, and it rises in shock even when the kidneys are unaffected. Lactate is also cleared largely by the liver, so hepatic dysfunction alters it independently of renal function.

questions.eli5: Low blood pressure alone is not the full definition of septic shock — the cells themselves must also be struggling to use oxygen. Lactate is the chemical that builds up when that happens, so it measures the second half of the definition. It is rechecked to see whether the treatment is actually reaching the tissues.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with HIV infection comes to the clinic to re-establish care after 3 years without treatment. He feels reasonably well but has had oral thrush twice in the past year and a 7-kg (15-lb) weight loss. His temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows white plaques on the buccal mucosa that scrape off, and mild generalized lymphadenopathy. His chest is clear and there is no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies show a CD4+ T-lymphocyte count of 88/μL and a plasma HIV RNA level of 210,000 copies/mL. A tuberculin skin test is negative, and a chest x-ray shows no abnormalities. Antiretroviral therapy is to be started. In addition, which of the following prophylactic regimens is indicated at this time?
choices: A. Azithromycin against disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex
B. Fluconazole against Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis
C. Isoniazid against latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection
D. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole against Pneumocystis jirovecii
E. Valganciclovir against cytomegalovirus retinitis
questions.explanation: The CD4 count tells you the DAMAGE and therefore who needs prophylaxis; the viral load tells you the ACTIVITY and drives transmission. Two CD4 thresholds matter and they are not the same number: BELOW 200/μL defines AIDS and is the threshold for Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis; BELOW 50/μL is where opportunistic infection risk is greatest. At 88/μL he is below 200 but above 50, so Pneumocystis prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is indicated — and that single agent conveniently also covers Toxoplasma gondii, whose own threshold is a CD4 below 100/μL with positive toxoplasma serology. Prophylaxis is stopped once antiretroviral therapy raises the CD4 count above the threshold durably. His recurrent thrush is a clinical marker of advancing immunosuppression, and watching for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome as his count recovers is part of the plan.

wrongExplanations.0: Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis was historically given below a CD4 count of 50/μL — he is at 88/μL, above that threshold. Current guidance has moved further still, deferring it in patients who are starting effective antiretroviral therapy, since suppressing the virus raises the count faster than macrolide prophylaxis adds benefit.
wrongExplanations.1: Routine primary prophylaxis against Cryptococcus is not recommended in the United States even at low CD4 counts. Fluconazole is used to TREAT established cryptococcal disease and as secondary prophylaxis afterward, not as primary prevention here.
wrongExplanations.2: Isoniazid preventive therapy is given for LATENT tuberculosis infection, which must first be demonstrated by a positive tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay. His skin test is negative and his chest x-ray is clear — though note that anergy at a low CD4 count can produce a false-negative result, which is why the test is repeated once the count recovers.
wrongExplanations.4: Cytomegalovirus prophylaxis is not routinely given even at very low counts; the standard approach is surveillance for symptoms, particularly retinitis, below a CD4 count of 50/μL. Valganciclovir is toxic and is reserved for treatment of established disease.

questions.eli5: How damaged the immune system is decides which infections he must be protected against, and that is measured by one number. Below 200 he needs protection against a specific lung infection; below 50 a different set of threats appears. He sits between those two, so he gets the first one — and the same pill covers a second parasite too.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the office because of pain and swelling of the left calf for 3 days. She began taking a combined oral contraceptive 8 months ago and smokes one pack of cigarettes daily. She has had no surgery, immobilization, travel, or trauma, and there is no family history of thrombosis. She takes no other medications. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a swollen, tender left calf. Compression ultrasonography confirms a thrombus in the left popliteal vein. She is treated with apixaban. She asks whether she will need to take an anticoagulant for the rest of her life. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
choices: A. Anticoagulation can likely be stopped after 3 months if the contraceptive is discontinued and she stops smoking
B. Indefinite anticoagulation is required because all unprovoked thromboses eventually recur
C. Indefinite anticoagulation is required because oral contraceptive use is a permanent and non-modifiable risk factor
D. The duration should be decided by thrombophilia testing performed while she is still taking the anticoagulant
E. The duration should be extended to 12 months and then guided by a repeat compression ultrasound of the leg
questions.explanation: Duration follows the CLOT, not the genotype — specifically, what provoked it and whether that provocation can be removed. Recurrence risk in the first year after stopping is roughly 3% after a major transient trigger such as surgery, 5% after a minor reversible one, and 10% when the event was unprovoked or the risk factor persists. Her event is PROVOKED, and provoked by something REVERSIBLE. The combination of a combined oral contraceptive and smoking carries a markedly elevated thrombotic risk, and that is exactly why identifying the combination matters more than anticoagulating around it: stopping both may remove the need for extended anticoagulation altogether. A provoked thrombosis with the provocation withdrawn is treated for 3 months. If instead she continued the contraceptive, the risk factor would be persistent and the calculus would change entirely.

wrongExplanations.1: This misstates both the fact and the category. Her thrombosis is not unprovoked — it has an identified reversible cause. And even genuinely unprovoked events are a judgement call rather than an automatic indefinite commitment, because the fatal recurrence rate of 0.3% to 1% per year overlaps the fatal bleeding rate of 0.2% to 0.6% per year.
wrongExplanations.2: Oral contraceptive use is the opposite of permanent — it is the most readily reversible risk factor she has, and she can simply stop it. Treating it as fixed would commit a 24-year-old to lifelong anticoagulation and its bleeding risk for no reason.
wrongExplanations.3: Thrombophilia testing should be sent only when the result would CHANGE what you do, and here it would not: she has a clear reversible provocation and the plan is already to stop it. Testing during anticoagulation is also unreliable — warfarin lowers proteins C and S, heparin lowers antithrombin, and acute thrombosis consumes natural anticoagulants, all of which generate false positives.
wrongExplanations.4: Extending to 12 months by default is not a recognized strategy, and duration is not decided by whether residual thrombus persists on ultrasound — most thrombi never fully resolve radiographically, so that would commit many patients to needless therapy. A persistently elevated D-dimer AFTER stopping is the marker that does carry recurrence information.

questions.eli5: Whether she stays on a blood thinner depends on why the clot happened and whether that reason can be removed. Hers was caused by the pill combined with smoking, and both can be stopped. Take away the cause and three months of treatment is enough.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 6-day history of cough, tachypnea, and poor feeding. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy but has been hospitalized twice for pneumonia and has had persistent oral thrush unresponsive to nystatin since 6 weeks of age. He is at the 3rd percentile for weight, having fallen from the 40th. His temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 168/min, and respirations are 66/min. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. Physical examination shows intercostal retractions, diffuse crackles, white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa, and NO palpable tonsillar tissue or cervical lymph nodes. A chest x-ray shows diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 4,100/mm3 with an absolute lymphocyte count of 480/mm3. Bronchoalveolar lavage with methenamine silver staining shows cup-shaped cysts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: A. Bruton agammaglobulinemia
B. Chronic granulomatous disease
C. DiGeorge syndrome
D. Selective IgA deficiency
E. Severe combined immunodeficiency
questions.explanation: TIMING separates the immunodeficiencies, and it does so for a mechanistic reason. Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and protects the infant for roughly the first 6 months — so a purely ANTIBODY defect stays silent until that transferred immunoglobulin wanes, then presents at about 6 months with pyogenic infections by encapsulated bacteria. Maternal antibody never covers the T-CELL arm at all, so a combined defect declares itself from about month 2 with OPPORTUNISTIC infection: persistent thrush, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (the cup-shaped cysts on silver stain here), chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. This infant fits the second pattern exactly, and the profound lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 480/mm3) confirms it. Absent tonsils and lymph nodes reflect the missing lymphoid mass. The block sits high on the maturation tree, before or at the divergence of the B and T lineages: X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency mutates the COMMON GAMMA CHAIN shared by several interleukin receptors, while the autosomal recessive form is adenosine deaminase deficiency, in which accumulated purines inhibit ribonucleotide reductase and kill rapidly dividing precursors. This is a pediatric emergency — no live vaccines, irradiated and cytomegalovirus-negative blood products only, and urgent transplant evaluation.

wrongExplanations.0: Bruton agammaglobulinemia also causes absent tonsils and lymph nodes, which makes it the most tempting alternative. It is excluded by timing and by organism: it presents AFTER about 6 months, once maternal IgG wanes, with pyogenic encapsulated bacteria — not with Pneumocystis and thrush at 6 weeks — and the absolute lymphocyte count is NORMAL, because T cells are intact.
wrongExplanations.1: Chronic granulomatous disease is a phagocyte disorder with absent NADPH oxidase, presenting with recurrent abscesses and infections by catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia, Nocardia, and Aspergillus. Lymphocyte counts and immunoglobulins are normal, and Pneumocystis is not characteristic.
wrongExplanations.2: DiGeorge syndrome from the 22q11.2 deletion is a purely CELLULAR deficiency from thymic hypoplasia and can cause opportunistic infection with lymphopenia. It is distinguished by its accompanying features — conotruncal cardiac defects, hypocalcemic seizures from parathyroid hypoplasia, and characteristic facies — none of which are described here, and a term infant with an uncomplicated course would be unusual.
wrongExplanations.3: Selective IgA deficiency is the most COMMON primary immunodeficiency but among the mildest: recurrent respiratory and gastrointestinal infections, often asymptomatic and found incidentally, with a risk of anaphylaxis to IgA-containing blood products. It does not cause lymphopenia, Pneumocystis pneumonia, or failure to thrive in infancy.

questions.eli5: Antibodies borrowed from his mother protect a baby for about the first six months, so a problem with antibodies alone stays hidden until then. Those borrowed antibodies never cover the other half of the immune system, so a baby missing that half gets unusual infections almost immediately. Thrush and this particular pneumonia at six weeks point straight there.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man is brought to the operating room for repair of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. Over 90 minutes he receives 14 units of packed red blood cells, 10 units of plasma, and 2 pools of platelets through a rapid infuser. His core temperature is maintained at 36.5°C. Toward the end of the procedure the anesthesiologist notes diffuse oozing from cut surfaces, and the electrocardiogram shows a prolonged QT interval. Pulse is 104/min and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                                  9.8 g/dL
    Platelet count                              118,000/mm3
    Prothrombin time                            15 sec (N=11–14)
    Fibrinogen                                  208 mg/dL (N=200–400)
    Ionized calcium                             0.71 mmol/L (N=1.10–1.30)
    Serum potassium                             5.1 mEq/L
    Arterial pH                                 7.30

Which of the following best explains the hypocalcemia?
choices: A. Chelation of calcium by citrate delivered with the transfused products
B. Dilution of calcium by the volume of transfused products
C. Precipitation of calcium phosphate from released intracellular phosphate
D. Redistribution of calcium into cells driven by the acidosis
E. Suppression of parathyroid hormone by the transfused volume
questions.explanation: Every unit of blood contains CITRATE as its anticoagulant, and citrate works by CHELATING CALCIUM — calcium is the trigger for the coagulation cascade, so without free calcium the unit cannot clot in the bag. Citrate is normally metabolized rapidly by the liver, so a routine transfusion causes no trouble. But during a MASSIVE transfusion the recipient receives a citrate load faster than the liver can clear it (and hepatic clearance is further impaired by hypoperfusion in shock), so the citrate begins chelating the PATIENT'S OWN calcium. The result is exactly what is described: a low ionized calcium with paresthesias, tetany, QT prolongation, hypotension from impaired myocardial contractility and vascular tone, and impaired hemostasis — because calcium is coagulation factor IV and the cascade cannot proceed without it. His oozing is therefore partly a calcium problem rather than purely a factor or platelet problem. Management is to monitor ionized calcium and replace it with intravenous calcium chloride or gluconate. Note that acidosis would ordinarily RAISE ionized calcium by displacing it from albumin, so his pH of 7.30 makes a measured value this low still more striking.

wrongExplanations.1: Simple dilution would lower many analytes proportionately, but the transfused products themselves contain calcium-binding citrate rather than calcium-free fluid, and dilution alone does not explain an ionized calcium this low. The mechanism is active chelation, not dilution.
wrongExplanations.2: Calcium phosphate precipitation driven by a high phosphate load is the mechanism of hypocalcemia in TUMOR LYSIS SYNDROME. There is no massive cell lysis here and no reported hyperphosphatemia; his mild hyperkalemia reflects stored-cell potassium leak and acidosis, not tumor lysis.
wrongExplanations.3: Acidosis shifts calcium in the OPPOSITE direction: hydrogen ions displace calcium from albumin binding sites, INCREASING the ionized fraction. That is why respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation can precipitate tetany. His acidemia should therefore be raising his ionized calcium, which makes the measured value even more clearly citrate-driven.
wrongExplanations.4: Parathyroid hormone actually RISES appropriately in response to a falling ionized calcium — the gland is responding correctly, not being suppressed. Transfused volume does not inhibit parathyroid function.

questions.eli5: Every bag of donated blood contains a chemical that grips calcium, because calcium is what makes blood clot — without it the bag would solidify. Given a few bags, the liver clears that chemical easily. Given fourteen bags in ninety minutes, it starts gripping the patient's own calcium instead, and calcium is needed for his heart and his clotting.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia is being counseled about prognosis before induction chemotherapy. He is otherwise fit, with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0. His marrow shows 62% myeloblasts. Cytogenetic and molecular studies are pending. Which of the following findings would most favorably affect his prognosis?
choices: A. A complex karyotype with five unrelated chromosomal abnormalities
B. A FLT3 internal tandem duplication with a high allelic ratio
C. Antecedent myelodysplastic syndrome
D. Monosomy 7
E. t(15;17) generating a PML-RARA fusion
questions.explanation: In the hematologic malignancies, CYTOGENETICS and molecular findings outweigh almost everything else, because they identify the mechanism and therefore the availability of a targeted therapy. t(15;17) generates the PML-RARA fusion of acute promyelocytic leukemia — a receptor that blocks myeloid differentiation at the promyelocyte stage. All-trans retinoic acid overcomes that block pharmacologically, forcing the malignant promyelocytes to MATURE rather than merely killing them, and combined with arsenic trioxide it converts what was once the most rapidly lethal subtype into the most curable, with survival around 90%. The danger is entirely front-loaded: the granules of those promyelocytes release procoagulant material and cause a disseminated intravascular coagulopathy that kills within days, which is why treatment is started ON SUSPICION before cytogenetics return. Every other option here is an adverse marker, and together they illustrate the general rule — complex karyotypes, monosomies, FLT3 internal tandem duplication, and disease arising out of a preceding marrow disorder all predict resistance and relapse.

wrongExplanations.0: A complex karyotype, conventionally three or more unrelated abnormalities, is among the strongest ADVERSE risk factors. It reflects widespread genomic instability, predicts poor response to induction, and generally indicates allogeneic transplantation in first remission.
wrongExplanations.1: FLT3 internal tandem duplication is an adverse molecular marker, and a high allelic ratio worsens it further. FLT3 is a receptor tyrosine kinase whose duplication leaves it constitutively active. It is targetable with inhibitors such as midostaurin, but it remains a poor-risk feature rather than a favorable one.
wrongExplanations.2: Acute myeloid leukemia arising from antecedent myelodysplastic syndrome — secondary disease — carries a distinctly worse prognosis than de novo disease. It reflects a marrow with pre-existing clonal damage, and roughly 30% of myelodysplastic syndrome progresses this way.
wrongExplanations.3: Monosomy 7 is a classic adverse cytogenetic finding, associated with therapy-related and secondary leukemia, with poor response to conventional chemotherapy.

questions.eli5: In blood cancers the specific genetic change matters more than almost anything else, because it says which drug will work. One particular chromosome swap makes a subtype that used to be the deadliest — but a vitamin A-based drug forces those cells to grow up instead of piling up. Recognized early, most patients are cured.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman who underwent right mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection and adjuvant radiation for breast cancer 3 years ago comes to the office because of gradually progressive swelling of the right arm over the past 8 months. The swelling is worse at the end of the day but never fully resolves overnight. She has had no pain, redness, fever, or shortness of breath. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 74/min, and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows non-pitting edema of the right arm and dorsum of the hand with thickened, doughy skin; the skin of the second finger CANNOT be tented at the base. There is no erythema, no cording, and no supraclavicular mass. Duplex ultrasonography of the right upper extremity shows no thrombus. Which of the following findings is most specific for this patient's diagnosis?
choices: A. Absence of thrombus on duplex ultrasonography of the arm
B. Inability to tent the skin at the base of the second finger
C. Non-pitting quality of the edema of the forearm and hand
D. Unilateral distribution of the swelling confined to the right arm
E. Worsening of the swelling through the course of the day
questions.explanation: This is the STEMMER SIGN, and it is the pathognomonic bedside finding of lymphedema. Protein-rich lymph accumulates in the interstitium and drives fibrosis of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, so the skin becomes thickened and tethered and can no longer be pinched up as a fold at the base of the digits — producing the characteristic squared-off appearance of the toes or fingers. A POSITIVE Stemmer sign (skin that cannot be tented) is highly specific; a negative sign points away from lymphedema. Her history supplies the mechanism: axillary lymph node dissection plus radiation is the commonest cause in developed countries, whereas FILARIASIS is the commonest cause worldwide. The clinical priority in any unilateral swollen limb is to exclude deep venous thrombosis first — because a thrombosis can kill and lymphedema cannot — which is why the duplex was done. Management is complete decongestive therapy: manual lymphatic drainage, compression, exercise, and meticulous skin care to prevent cellulitis, which each episode makes more likely.

wrongExplanations.0: A negative duplex is essential and it excludes the dangerous competing diagnosis, but excluding one condition is not the same as being specific FOR another. Many causes of a swollen arm have no thrombus, including recurrent tumor, infection, and dependency.
wrongExplanations.2: Non-pitting edema is characteristic of established lymphedema and is a useful clue, but it is not specific: myxedema and chronic venous disease with fibrosis can also produce non-pitting swelling, and EARLY lymphedema pits before fibrosis develops.
wrongExplanations.3: Unilateral distribution correctly narrows the differential toward a local process and away from systemic causes such as heart, liver, or kidney disease. But deep venous thrombosis, cellulitis, and recurrent axillary tumor are all unilateral too, so it does not discriminate among them.
wrongExplanations.4: Diurnal worsening reflects gravity-dependent fluid accumulation and occurs in venous insufficiency and dependent edema as well. In lymphedema it is a helpful historical feature — particularly that it does NOT fully resolve overnight — but it is not specific.

questions.eli5: When lymph fluid cannot drain it stays trapped and slowly turns the skin thick and leathery. A doctor tests this by trying to pinch up a fold of skin at the base of a finger or toe — in this condition the skin is too tethered to lift. That single bedside test is the giveaway.
